opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about it in a few layers. At the top there's a fairly simple north star: we want to build systems that can do increasingly autonomous, useful intellectual work, and eventually help accelerate scientific discovery itself. Everything else should ladder up to that.

Underneath that, I'd split the roadmap into two broad buckets. The first is what I'd call the core scaling bets: pretraining, reinforcement learning, and reasoning. These are the engines of capability. A lot of my job is making sure we're placing the right-sized bets there, and that we're not over-indexing on whatever looked exciting last quarter. Pretraining gives you a broad, rich world model, and RL and reasoning teach the model to use that knowledge deliberately and over longer horizons. The interplay between the two is where a lot of the interesting research is right now.

The second bucket is the more exploratory work: new architectures, new data regimes, new ways of doing evaluation, and things that might look a little crazy today. We deliberately protect some fraction of compute and people for that, because history says the next paradigm usually starts out looking like a side project.

Then there's a cross-cutting layer. Safety and alignment, infrastructure, and evals aren't separate from capabilities. They're what lets you actually trust and ship what you've built. If your evals are bad, you're flying blind, and if your infra can't keep up, your research ideas don't matter.

Culturally, the thing I try to emphasize is conviction plus humility. You need strong conviction to commit serious compute to a direction for months, but you also need to be willing to look at the results honestly and say, "This isn't working, let's move." The roadmap is less of a fixed plan and more of a portfolio we keep rebalancing as we learn.

r001.rationale: The response says pretraining builds a broad world model, then RL and reasoning teach the model to use that knowledge deliberately over longer horizons.

r002.rationale: The response describes core scaling bets and exploratory research, but does not say the new bets aim to change scaling properties.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, there are really two big pillars, and then a lot of things that hang off those pillars.

The first pillar is pretraining. That's the thing that gives you a base model that knows a lot about the world, and we're still very much in the business of scaling that up and making it more efficient. The second pillar is reasoning, which is essentially the reinforcement learning paradigm that started with the o-series. That's about teaching the model to spend compute at test time, to think longer, to check its work, to use tools. A lot of the excitement over the last couple of years has been realizing those two things compound. A better base model gives you a better starting point for RL, and better RL gives you a model that can generate better data and better evaluations, which feeds back into the next pretraining run.

Then there are a few things that cut across both. One is multimodality, because we don't think intelligence stops at text. Vision, audio, video, and eventually acting in the world all matter. Another is agents, which is really the question of how you take a model that can reason well in a single turn and get it to do long-horizon work reliably, with memory, with tool use, with the ability to recover when something goes wrong. And then there's alignment and safety, which I don't think of as a separate roadmap so much as a constraint on all of it. If you can't understand and steer what the model is doing, the capabilities don't actually translate into something useful.

The way we organize the org reflects this. You have teams that are deep on a frontier, like pretraining scale or RL algorithms, and you have teams that are closer to the product and are constantly surfacing where the models fall short in practice. The hard part of my job is making sure the failures people see in the real world actually make it back into the research agenda, and that the research bets we make are the ones that will matter in two or three years, not just the ones that look good on a benchmark next quarter.

So if I had to compress it: scale the base, scale the reasoning, make them work together, and then make the whole thing safe and usable enough that it changes how people actually get things done.

r001.rationale: The response describes reasoning as reinforcement learning that teaches models to spend compute at test time, and says a pretrained base model provides a better starting point for RL.

r002.rationale: It mentions scaling pretraining, test-time compute, and compounding gains, but does not identify changing scaling properties as an aim of OpenAI’s research bets.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as a few connected directions. One is pushing the capabilities of the models: can they reason through harder problems, learn more efficiently, and work across different kinds of inputs? Another is making those capabilities useful—getting from a model that gives you a good answer to a system that can help you carry out a task reliably.

Then there’s the question of how we know we’re making progress. As tasks get more complex, evaluating success gets harder, and safety and reliability have to develop alongside capability.

Those directions feed into each other. Research opens up new things people can do, and seeing where the systems succeed or struggle gives us a much better sense of what to work on next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reasoning and model capabilities but does not present reinforcement learning as teaching models to reason with knowledge acquired through pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as a few connected questions. How do we make the models more capable? How do we make those capabilities reliable and useful? And how do we make sure that, as the models become more powerful, we can understand and steer their behavior?

Those questions feed into each other. You can make progress on a research benchmark, but putting a model in people’s hands exposes a different set of limitations. Maybe it knows how to solve a problem but doesn’t consistently follow through, or it needs to use a tool and recover when something goes wrong. That feedback helps shape the next research questions.

So there’s a long-term direction toward more general intelligence, but the roadmap isn’t a single straight line. It’s a portfolio of research bets, with a pretty tight loop between fundamental research, safety work, and what we learn from deployment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses model capability and feedback from deployment but does not present reinforcement learning as teaching models to reason with pre-training knowledge.

r002.rationale: It describes a portfolio of research bets, but does not identify changing scaling properties as an aim.
